question: In the expression \(\omega=2\pi f\), the quantity \(\omega\) is called
explanation: Angular frequency \(\omega\) gives the rate of change of phase with time. It is related to ordinary frequency \(f\) by \(\omega=2\pi f\). The factor \(2\pi\) appears because one complete oscillation corresponds to \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\) of phase. Wavelength \(\lambda\) is a spatial repeat distance, while wave number \(k\) is related to wavelength by \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\). Linear mass density \(\mu\) belongs to waves on strings and is not a time-rate of phase. The unit of \(\omega\) is commonly written as \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

question: A periodic wave has frequency \(50\,\text{Hz}\). Its angular frequency is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Frequency \(f=50\,\text{Hz}=50\,\text{s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Angular frequency \(\omega\).
\( \textbf{Relation:} \)
\[
\omega=2\pi f
\]
This relation converts cycles per second into radians of phase per second.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\omega=2\pi(50\,\text{s}^{-1})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\omega=100\pi\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit writing:} \)
\[
\omega=100\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The angular frequency is \(100\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).
Forgetting the factor \(2\pi\) would confuse ordinary frequency with angular frequency.

question: The wave number \(k\) of a sinusoidal wave is related to wavelength by
explanation: Wave number \(k\) measures how rapidly the phase changes with position. One full wavelength \(\lambda\) corresponds to a phase change of \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\). Therefore, phase change per unit distance is \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\). The unit of \(k\) is commonly \(\text{rad m}^{-1}\), or simply \(\text{m}^{-1}\) when radian is treated as dimensionless. The expression \(f\lambda\) gives wave speed \(v\), not wave number. A larger wavelength means a smaller value of \(k\), because the phase changes more slowly with distance.

question: A sinusoidal wave has wavelength \(0.40\,\text{m}\). The wave number is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Wavelength \(\lambda=0.40\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Wave number \(k\).
\( \textbf{Relation used:} \)
\[
k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}
\]
This relation gives phase change per unit distance.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
k=\frac{2\pi}{0.40\,\text{m}}
\]
\( \textbf{Decimal handling:} \)
\[
0.40=\frac{2}{5}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
k=2\pi\times\frac{5}{2}=5\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave number is \(5\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}\).
The reciprocal dependence means a shorter wavelength gives a larger wave number.

question: In a progressive sinusoidal wave, the phase may contain the term \(kx-\omega t+\phi\). The role of \(\phi\) is to represent
opt_b: linear mass density of the string
explanation: The phase of a sinusoidal wave decides the stage of oscillation at a given position and time. In \(kx-\omega t+\phi\), the terms \(kx\) and \(\omega t\) describe how phase changes with position and time. The term \(\phi\) is a constant added to set the starting phase of the wave. It can shift the wave pattern without changing the amplitude, frequency, or wavelength. Linear mass density \(\mu\), particle speed, and pressure are different physical quantities. The phase constant helps locate the wave in its cycle at the chosen origin of \(x\) and \(t\).

question:
Study the table and identify the mismatched quantity-unit pair.

PAngular frequency \(\omega\)\(\text{rad s}^{-1}\)
QWave number \(k\)\(\text{m}^{-1}\)
RFrequency \(f\)\(\text{Hz}\)
SWavelength \(\lambda\)\(\text{s}^{-1}\)
explanation: Wavelength \(\lambda\) is a distance, so its unit is \(\text{m}\), not \(\text{s}^{-1}\). Row P is suitable because angular frequency \(\omega\) is measured in \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\). Row Q is suitable because wave number \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\) has unit \(\text{m}^{-1}\). Row R is suitable because frequency \(f\) is measured in \(\text{Hz}\), which is \(\text{s}^{-1}\). The mismatched row confuses a spatial period with a rate in time. Keeping \(\lambda\), \(f\), \(\omega\), and \(k\) separated is essential before using a progressive wave equation.

question: In the phase expression \(kx-\omega t+\phi\), the term \(kx\) is dimensionless because
opt_d: \(k\) has unit \(\text{kg m}^{-1}\) and \(x\) has unit \(\text{kg}\)
explanation: The argument of a sine or cosine function must be dimensionless. In the phase term \(kx\), the coordinate \(x\) is a length and has unit \(\text{m}\). Therefore \(k\) must have the reciprocal length unit \(\text{m}^{-1}\), often written as \(\text{rad m}^{-1}\). Multiplying \(k\) and \(x\) gives a pure phase angle in radians. Similarly, \(\omega t\) is dimensionless because \(\omega\) has unit \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\) and \(t\) has unit \(\text{s}\). Dimensional consistency is a reliable way to separate wave number from angular frequency.

question: A sinusoidal wave has time period \(0.020\,\text{s}\) and wavelength \(0.50\,\text{m}\). The values of \(\omega\) and \(k\) are respectively
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Time period \(T=0.020\,\text{s}\), wavelength \(\lambda=0.50\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Angular frequency relation:} \)
\[
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution for \(\omega\):} \)
\[
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{0.020\,\text{s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation for \(\omega\):} \)
\[
\omega=100\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Wave number relation:} \)
\[
k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution for \(k\):} \)
\[
k=\frac{2\pi}{0.50\,\text{m}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation for \(k\):} \)
\[
k=4\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\omega=100\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\) and \(k=4\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}\).
The time period controls \(\omega\), while the wavelength controls \(k\).

question: A phase constant \(\phi\) is changed in the equation of a sinusoidal wave, while \(A\), \(k\), and \(\omega\) remain the same. The change mainly
opt_a: changes only the initial phase of the wave
opt_b: changes the wave speed by changing the medium
explanation: The phase constant \(\phi\) fixes the phase of the wave at the chosen origin of position and time. If \(A\), \(k\), and \(\omega\) remain unchanged, the amplitude, wavelength, and frequency remain unchanged. Changing \(\phi\) shifts the sinusoidal pattern in its cycle. It does not represent a change of medium or a change of propagation speed by itself. Since \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\), unchanged \(k\) means unchanged \(\lambda\). Since \(\omega=2\pi f\), unchanged \(\omega\) means unchanged \(f\).

question: The phase of a sinusoidal wave at a point changes by \(6\pi\,\text{rad}\) in \(0.30\,\text{s}\). The angular frequency is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given phase change:} \) \(\Delta \theta=6\pi\,\text{rad}\).
\( \textbf{Time interval:} \) \(\Delta t=0.30\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Angular frequency \(\omega\).
\( \textbf{Meaning of angular frequency:} \) It is the rate of change of phase with time.
\[
\omega=\frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\omega=\frac{6\pi\,\text{rad}}{0.30\,\text{s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\omega=20\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The angular frequency is \(20\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).
This calculation uses phase change, not distance travelled by the wave.

question: A phase changes by \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\) when position changes by one wavelength. This statement leads to
explanation: Wave number \(k\) measures phase change per unit distance. A complete spatial cycle of a sinusoidal wave corresponds to a phase change of \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\). The distance for one complete spatial cycle is the wavelength \(\lambda\). Therefore, phase change per unit distance is \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\). The relation \(\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}\) is similar in form, but it concerns phase change with time. The given statement is spatial, so it points to \(k\), not \(\omega\).

S\(\lambda\)Number of oscillations per second
The mismatched row is
explanation: Row S is mismatched because \(\lambda\) is wavelength, the spatial distance between nearest points in the same phase. The number of oscillations per second is frequency \(f\), not wavelength. Row P is suitable because \(\omega\) gives phase change per unit time. Row Q is suitable because \(k\) gives phase change per unit position. Row R is suitable because \(\phi\) sets a constant shift in phase. The mismatch replaces a spatial quantity with a time-rate quantity.

question: A wave is described by a phase \(kx-\omega t+\phi\). At fixed \(x\), increasing \(t\) changes the phase mainly through the term
explanation: At fixed \(x\), the value of \(kx\) remains constant because the position is not changing. The phase constant \(\phi\) also remains fixed. The time variation of the phase is therefore controlled by the term involving \(t\), namely \(-\omega t\). The angular frequency \(\omega\) tells how quickly the phase changes with time at that fixed position. The product \(k\omega\) is not a separate term in the given phase expression. This is why a \(y-t\) graph at one position is connected with \(\omega\) and \(T\).

question: A wave has \(\omega=40\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\) and \(k=5\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}\). Its wave speed is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(\omega=40\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), \(k=5\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Wave speed \(v\).
\( \textbf{Relation between phase constants and speed:} \)
\[
v=\frac{\omega}{k}
\]
This follows because \(\omega\) measures phase change per unit time and \(k\) measures phase change per unit distance.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=\frac{40\pi\,\text{s}^{-1}}{5\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Cancellation:} \)
\[
\frac{40\pi}{5\pi}=8
\]
\( \textbf{Unit check:} \)
\[
\frac{\text{s}^{-1}}{\text{m}^{-1}}=\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed is \(8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
The factors of \(\pi\) cancel because both \(\omega\) and \(k\) are phase-rate quantities.

question: The relation \(v=\frac{\omega}{k}\) is consistent with \(v=f\lambda\) because
explanation: The angular frequency is related to ordinary frequency by \(\omega=2\pi f\). The wave number is related to wavelength by \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\). Substituting these in \(v=\frac{\omega}{k}\) gives \(v=\frac{2\pi f}{2\pi/\lambda}\). The factor \(2\pi\) cancels, leaving \(v=f\lambda\). This shows that both forms describe the same wave speed. The relation \(v=\frac{\omega}{k}\) uses phase rates, while \(v=f\lambda\) uses cycles and wavelength.

question: A travelling wave enters a second part of a string where the wave speed becomes smaller, while the source frequency remains unchanged. The wavelength in the second part
opt_b: decreases because \(f\) stays fixed and \(v\) decreases
opt_c: remains unchanged because wavelength is fixed only by the source
opt_d: becomes zero because the wave crosses a boundary
explanation: When a wave crosses into a new medium, the source frequency remains the same because the source continues to oscillate at the same rate. The wave speed, however, depends on the medium. The relation \(v=f\lambda\) then shows that if \(v\) decreases while \(f\) stays fixed, \(\lambda\) must decrease. The wavelength adjusts to match the speed in the new medium. It is not fixed only by the source. The frequency is the source-controlled quantity, while the speed is medium-controlled for a mechanical wave.

question: A wave source produces waves of frequency \(12\,\text{Hz}\) in a medium where the wave speed is \(36\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). If the same source produces waves in another medium where the speed is \(24\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), the new wavelength is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given source frequency:} \) \(f=12\,\text{Hz}=12\,\text{s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{New medium speed:} \) \(v_2=24\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) New wavelength \(\lambda_2\).
\( \textbf{Relation used:} \)
\[
v=f\lambda
\]
The source frequency is unchanged when the same source drives waves in the second medium.
\( \textbf{Rearranging:} \)
\[
\lambda_2=\frac{v_2}{f}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\lambda_2=\frac{24\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{12\,\text{s}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\lambda_2=2.0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The new wavelength is \(2.0\,\text{m}\).
The earlier speed \(36\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) is useful for comparison, but the new wavelength must use the new medium speed.

question: A periodic wave has frequency \(6.0\,\text{Hz}\) and wavelength \(0.75\,\text{m}\). Another wave in the same medium has frequency \(9.0\,\text{Hz}\). If the medium fixes the speed, the wavelength of the second wave is
explanation:
\( \textbf{First wave data:} \) \(f_1=6.0\,\text{Hz}\), \(\lambda_1=0.75\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Medium condition:} \) Both waves are in the same medium, so the wave speed is the same.
\( \textbf{Speed from first wave:} \)
\[
v=f_1\lambda_1
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=(6.0\,\text{s}^{-1})(0.75\,\text{m})=4.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Second wave frequency:} \) \(f_2=9.0\,\text{Hz}\).
\( \textbf{Wavelength of second wave:} \)
\[
\lambda_2=\frac{v}{f_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\lambda_2=\frac{4.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{9.0\,\text{s}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\lambda_2=0.50\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wavelength of the second wave is \(0.50\,\text{m}\).
In the same medium, a higher frequency corresponds to a shorter wavelength.

question:
A table compares two cases for waves in the same medium.
CaseFrequencyWavelength
P\(f\)\(\lambda\)
Q\(2f\)\(\frac{\lambda}{2}\)
The table is based on the condition that
opt_d: wavelength is independent of frequency in the same medium
explanation: For a wave in the same medium, the propagation speed is usually fixed by the medium conditions. The relation \(v=f\lambda\) must then remain constant. If frequency becomes \(2f\), the wavelength must become \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\) so that the product \(f\lambda\) is unchanged. The time period does not remain the same, because doubling frequency halves the time period. The table therefore represents inverse change of \(f\) and \(\lambda\) at constant \(v\). It does not show wavelength being independent of frequency.

question:
Assertion: For mechanical waves in a given uniform medium, changing the source frequency does not by itself change the wave speed.
Reason: In a given medium, the wave speed is determined by the medium’s physical properties.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The Assertion is true for the usual school-level treatment of mechanical waves in a fixed uniform medium. Changing the source frequency changes how often wave crests or compressions are produced. The wave speed is controlled by the medium’s properties, such as tension and linear mass density for a string. If the speed remains fixed, the wavelength adjusts according to \(v=f\lambda\). The Reason correctly states why frequency change alone does not decide the speed in a given medium. The source controls \(f\), while the medium controls \(v\).

question: A wave is described by \(f=20\,\text{Hz}\) and \(\lambda=0.30\,\text{m}\). The same wave may also be described by \(\omega\) and \(k\). The ratio \(\frac{\omega}{k}\) equals
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(f=20\,\text{Hz}\), \(\lambda=0.30\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) \(\frac{\omega}{k}\).
\( \textbf{Phase-speed relation:} \)
\[
\frac{\omega}{k}=v
\]
\( \textbf{Cycle-based speed relation:} \)
\[
v=f\lambda
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=(20\,\text{s}^{-1})(0.30\,\text{m})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
v=6.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Therefore:} \)
\[
\frac{\omega}{k}=6.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The ratio \(\frac{\omega}{k}\) equals \(6.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
The ratio of phase rates gives the same propagation speed as \(f\lambda\).

question: A wave travelling from one medium into another has its frequency unchanged but its wavelength changes from \(0.40\,\text{m}\) to \(0.25\,\text{m}\). If the original speed was \(12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), the new speed is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Original data:} \) \(v_1=12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(\lambda_1=0.40\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{New wavelength:} \) \(\lambda_2=0.25\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Boundary condition:} \) The frequency remains unchanged.
\( \textbf{Original frequency:} \)
\[
f=\frac{v_1}{\lambda_1}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
f=\frac{12\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{0.40\,\text{m}}=30\,\text{Hz}
\]
\( \textbf{New speed relation:} \)
\[
v_2=f\lambda_2
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v_2=(30\,\text{s}^{-1})(0.25\,\text{m})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
v_2=7.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The new speed is \(7.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
A shorter wavelength at unchanged frequency means a smaller wave speed.

question: A claim says, “When a wave enters a new medium, its frequency must change because its speed changes.” The best correction is that
opt_a: the speed is fixed by the source, while the frequency adjusts randomly
opt_b: both frequency and wavelength must become zero at the boundary
opt_c: frequency and wavelength are always independent of wave speed
opt_d: frequency is fixed by the source, while wavelength adjusts to speed
explanation: The source decides how often wave disturbances are produced, so it fixes the frequency. When the wave enters a new medium, the propagation speed may change because the medium properties are different. The relation \(v=f\lambda\) must still hold in the new medium. Since \(f\) remains the same, \(\lambda\) changes to match the new value of \(v\). This is why wave speed changes at a boundary are usually accompanied by wavelength changes, not source-frequency changes. The boundary does not create a new source frequency by itself.

question: A graph is drawn between wave speed \(v\) and wavelength \(\lambda\) for waves of a fixed frequency \(f\). The graph should be
opt_a: a straight line through the origin with slope \(f\)
opt_b: a straight line through the origin with slope \(\frac{1}{f}\)
opt_c: a horizontal line because \(v\) never changes
explanation:
\( \textbf{Fixed quantity:} \) The frequency \(f\) is constant.
\( \textbf{Wave speed relation:} \)
\[
v=f\lambda
\]
\( \textbf{Graph variables:} \) The vertical axis is \(v\), and the horizontal axis is \(\lambda\).
\( \textbf{Comparison with straight-line form:} \)
\[
v=(f)\lambda
\]
This matches the form \(y=mx\), where the slope is \(f\).
\( \textbf{Intercept:} \) When \(\lambda=0\), the mathematical relation gives \(v=0\), so the line passes through the origin.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The graph is a straight line through the origin with slope \(f\).
The inverse graph idea would apply to \(\lambda\) versus \(f\) only when \(v\) is fixed.

question: A travelling disturbance has shape \(F(x)\) at \(t=0\). After time \(t\), the same shape has shifted a distance \(vt\) toward positive \(x\) without changing form. Its displacement can be written as
explanation: A wave travelling toward positive \(x\) carries the same profile forward with time. If a particular part of the profile was at position \(x_0\) at \(t=0\), then after time \(t\) it is found at \(x=x_0+vt\). Rearranging gives \(x_0=x-vt\). Therefore, the displacement at \((x,t)\) is the old profile value \(F(x-vt)\). The quantity \(x-vt\) remains constant for a fixed part of the moving profile. The minus sign does not mean motion toward negative \(x\); it is the sign required for a profile moving toward positive \(x\).

question: A wave profile is represented by \(y=F(x+vt)\). As time increases, a point of constant shape satisfies \(x+vt=\text{constant}\). The direction of propagation is
explanation: A fixed part of the profile is found by keeping the argument of \(F\) constant. For \(y=F(x+vt)\), constant profile condition is \(x+vt=C\), where \(C\) is a constant. Rearranging gives \(x=C-vt\). As \(t\) increases, \(x\) decreases. This means the same part of the wave profile moves toward the negative \(x\)-direction. The plus sign inside the argument therefore corresponds to negative \(x\)-direction propagation.

question: A pulse on a string is described at \(t=0\) by \(y=F(x)\). It travels toward positive \(x\) with speed \(3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). After \(2.0\,\text{s}\), the point of the pulse that was originally at \(x=1.0\,\text{m}\) will be at
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Initial position of a point on the profile \(x_0=1.0\,\text{m}\), speed \(v=3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), time \(t=2.0\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Direction:} \) The pulse travels toward positive \(x\).
\( \textbf{Translation relation:} \)
\[
x=x_0+vt
\]
\( \textbf{Why this applies:} \) A travelling pulse shifts its profile without changing shape in the ideal description.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
x=1.0\,\text{m}+(3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1})(2.0\,\text{s})
\]
\( \textbf{Intermediate calculation:} \)
\[
vt=6.0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final position:} \)
\[
x=1.0\,\text{m}+6.0\,\text{m}=7.0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The point of the pulse is at \(x=7.0\,\text{m}\).
Using \(x_0-vt\) would describe motion toward negative \(x\), not the stated direction.

question: A wave moving along a straight line keeps its shape unchanged. The statement “profile translation without distortion” means that
opt_a: the graph changes amplitude randomly as it translates through the medium
opt_b: each part of the graph shifts equally along the propagation direction
opt_c: the medium particles are permanently transported with the graph
opt_d: the wavelength becomes zero after the graph shifts
explanation: A travelling wave written as \(F(x-vt)\) or \(F(x+vt)\) represents the same shape shifted along the \(x\)-axis. If the wave is ideal and non-dispersive in this description, the profile does not change form while moving. Every identifiable part of the profile, such as a crest or pulse maximum, shifts by the same distance in the same time. This is different from permanent transport of the medium, because the particles may only oscillate locally. The mathematical argument \(x\mp vt\) is designed to express this translation. Shape preservation is the key idea, not random amplitude change.

question: A disturbance is described by \(y=F(x-4t)\), where \(x\) is in \(\text{m}\) and \(t\) is in \(\text{s}\). The propagation speed and direction are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given wave form:} \) \(y=F(x-4t)\).
\( \textbf{Standard form:} \) A wave travelling toward positive \(x\) can be written as \(y=F(x-vt)\).
\( \textbf{Comparison:} \)
\[
x-4t=x-vt
\]
\( \textbf{Speed identification:} \)
\[
v=4\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction identification:} \) The minus sign before \(vt\) corresponds to motion toward positive \(x\).
\( \textbf{Constant-profile check:} \)
\[
x-4t=C \Rightarrow x=C+4t
\]
As \(t\) increases, \(x\) increases.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave travels with speed \(4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) toward positive \(x\).
The coefficient of \(t\) has the unit of speed because it must multiply time to form a length.

question: A travelling wave is represented by \(y=F(x+6t)\), with \(x\) in \(\text{m}\) and \(t\) in \(\text{s}\). A point of fixed profile is at \(x=2.0\,\text{m}\) when \(t=0\). Its position at \(t=0.50\,\text{s}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given wave form:} \) \(y=F(x+6t)\).
\( \textbf{Fixed profile condition:} \)
\[
x+6t=C
\]
\( \textbf{Initial condition:} \) At \(t=0\), \(x=2.0\,\text{m}\), so
\[
C=2.0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Position at \(t=0.50\,\text{s}\):} \)
\[
x+6(0.50)=2.0
\]
\( \textbf{Intermediate value:} \)
\[
6(0.50)=3.0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Solving:} \)
\[
x=2.0\,\text{m}-3.0\,\text{m}=-1.0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The fixed part of the profile is at \(x=-1.0\,\text{m}\).
The plus sign in \(x+6t\) makes the fixed profile move toward smaller \(x\).

question: A student writes that \(F(x-vt)\) must represent a wave travelling toward negative \(x\) because of the minus sign. The best correction is that
opt_b: \(F(x-vt)\) represents no motion because \(x\) and \(t\) cancel
opt_d: \(F(x-vt)\) is impossible because the argument has units
explanation: The sign in the argument must be interpreted using the constant-profile condition. For \(F(x-vt)\), a fixed part of the shape has \(x-vt=C\). Therefore \(x=C+vt\), so the position of that part increases with time. This indicates motion toward positive \(x\). The expression is not a standing wave because it describes a single profile translating through space. The argument \(x-vt\) has units of length, which is suitable as input to a shape function \(F\). The apparent minus sign is less important than how \(x\) changes when the argument is held constant.

The fully correct pair of rows is
explanation: A profile of the form \(F(x-vt)\) travels toward positive \(x\). This follows from \(x-vt=C\), which gives \(x=C+vt\). A profile of the form \(F(x+vt)\) travels toward negative \(x\). This follows from \(x+vt=C\), which gives \(x=C-vt\). Row R is wrong because \(F(x-vt)\) does represent propagation. Row S reverses the direction associated with \(F(x+vt)\). The correct direction is found by holding the profile argument constant.

question: A sinusoidal wave travelling in the positive \(x\)-direction is most commonly represented as
explanation: A sinusoidal progressive wave travelling toward positive \(x\) has phase of the form \(kx-\omega t+\phi\). The condition of constant phase gives \(kx-\omega t+\phi=C\). Rearranging shows that \(x\) increases as \(t\) increases, so the wave travels toward positive \(x\). The amplitude \(A\) multiplies the sine function and gives maximum displacement. The quantities \(k\) and \(\omega\) control spatial and time phase changes respectively. Interchanging \(k\) and \(\omega\) would also make the units inside the phase wrong.

question: The equation \(y=A\sin(kx+\omega t+\phi)\) represents a sinusoidal wave travelling in
opt_d: no direction because sine waves cannot travel
explanation: The direction is obtained from the constant phase condition. For \(y=A\sin(kx+\omega t+\phi)\), a fixed phase satisfies \(kx+\omega t+\phi=C\). Rearranging gives \(x=\frac{C-\phi-\omega t}{k}\). As \(t\) increases, \(x\) decreases if \(k\) and \(\omega\) are positive. This means the phase point moves toward the negative \(x\)-direction. The wave may have displacement in \(y\), but its propagation direction is decided by the movement of phase along \(x\).

question: A sinusoidal wave is written as \(y=0.020\sin(4\pi x-20\pi t)\), where \(x\) is in \(\text{m}\), \(t\) is in \(\text{s}\), and \(y\) is in \(\text{m}\). The amplitude, wavelength, and frequency are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given equation:} \)
\[
y=0.020\sin(4\pi x-20\pi t)
\]
\( \textbf{Standard form:} \)
\[
y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Amplitude:} \)
\[
A=0.020\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Wave number:} \)
\[
k=4\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Wavelength relation:} \)
\[
\lambda=\frac{2\pi}{k}=\frac{2\pi}{4\pi}=0.50\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Angular frequency:} \)
\[
\omega=20\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Frequency relation:} \)
\[
f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}=\frac{20\pi}{2\pi}=10\,\text{Hz}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(A=0.020\,\text{m}\), \(\lambda=0.50\,\text{m}\), and \(f=10\,\text{Hz}\).
The coefficients of \(x\) and \(t\) are \(k\) and \(\omega\), not the wavelength and frequency themselves.

question: For the wave \(y=0.030\sin(5x-15t)\), where \(x\) is in \(\text{m}\) and \(t\) is in \(\text{s}\), the wave speed is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given equation:} \)
\[
y=0.030\sin(5x-15t)
\]
\( \textbf{Standard comparison:} \)
\[
y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Identify phase constants:} \)
\[
k=5\,\text{m}^{-1},\quad \omega=15\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Wave speed relation:} \)
\[
v=\frac{\omega}{k}
\]
This relation applies to a sinusoidal travelling wave because speed is the rate at which a fixed phase point moves.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=\frac{15\,\text{s}^{-1}}{5\,\text{m}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
v=3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed is \(3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Multiplying \(k\) and \(\omega\) would not give the unit of speed.

question: A sinusoidal wave travelling toward negative \(x\) has amplitude \(A\), wave number \(k\), angular frequency \(\omega\), and zero phase constant. The suitable equation is
explanation: A negative \(x\)-direction sinusoidal wave has the phase form \(kx+\omega t+\phi\). With zero phase constant, this becomes \(kx+\omega t\). Holding the phase constant gives \(kx+\omega t=C\), so \(x\) decreases as \(t\) increases. That is the mathematical sign of propagation toward negative \(x\). The form \(kx-\omega t\) corresponds to positive \(x\)-direction propagation. The terms inside the sine must also be dimensionless phase terms, so \(kx\) and \(\omega t\) are the valid combinations.

question: A graph of a sinusoidal wave is compared at \(t=0\) and a later time \(t_1\). The entire graph has shifted to the right, while its shape and amplitude are unchanged. A suitable phase form is
explanation: A rightward shift means that the wave is propagating toward positive \(x\). For a positive \(x\)-direction sinusoidal wave, the phase has the form \(kx-\omega t+\phi\). The constant phase condition then gives increasing \(x\) as time increases. The form \(kx+\omega t+\phi\) would shift the pattern toward negative \(x\). The unchanged shape and amplitude show that the wave is being translated rather than deformed. The signs inside the phase decide the direction of the moving pattern.

question: A sinusoidal wave is represented by \(y=0.050\sin(2\pi x+8\pi t+\frac{\pi}{3})\). The direction of propagation and phase constant are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given equation:} \)
\[
y=0.050\sin\left(2\pi x+8\pi t+\frac{\pi}{3}\right)
\]
\( \textbf{Standard negative-direction form:} \)
\[
y=A\sin(kx+\omega t+\phi)
\]
\( \textbf{Direction decision:} \) The sign between \(kx\) and \(\omega t\) is plus, so the wave travels toward negative \(x\).
\( \textbf{Phase constant:} \) The constant term in the phase is
\[
\phi=\frac{\pi}{3}
\]
\( \textbf{Other coefficients:} \) \(2\pi\) is \(k\), and \(8\pi\) is \(\omega\), not the phase constant.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave travels toward negative \(x\) and has phase constant \(\frac{\pi}{3}\).
The sign of the time term decides direction, while the constant term shifts the phase.

question: In the equation \(y=A\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi)\), increasing \(A\) while keeping \(k\), \(\omega\), and \(\phi\) unchanged will
opt_c: reverse the direction of wave propagation
explanation: The amplitude \(A\) is the maximum displacement of a medium particle from its mean position. In the equation \(y=A\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi)\), \(A\) multiplies the sine function and controls the vertical scale of displacement. The wavelength is controlled by \(k\), since \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\). The frequency is controlled by \(\omega\), since \(\omega=2\pi f\). The direction is decided by the sign between \(kx\) and \(\omega t\). Changing \(A\) alone changes the size of oscillation, not the wave’s phase pattern in space and time.

question: A wave equation contains the phase \(3x-12t\). Another possible phase \(3x+12t\) is written using the same \(k\) and \(\omega\). The main difference between the two waves is
explanation: Both phase expressions have the same coefficient of \(x\), so both have the same wave number \(k=3\,\text{m}^{-1}\). Both have the same magnitude of the coefficient of \(t\), so both have the same angular frequency \(\omega=12\,\text{s}^{-1}\). Since \(k\) and \(\omega\) have the same magnitudes, the wavelength, frequency, and speed magnitudes are the same. The sign between the spatial and time terms is different. The phase \(3x-12t\) represents positive \(x\)-direction propagation, while \(3x+12t\) represents negative \(x\)-direction propagation. The sign changes the direction, not the amplitude.

question: A wave is described by \(y=0.010\sin(10\pi x-40\pi t)\). How far does a fixed phase point of this wave move in \(0.25\,\text{s}\)?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given equation:} \)
\[
y=0.010\sin(10\pi x-40\pi t)
\]
\( \textbf{Identify constants:} \)
\[
k=10\pi\,\text{m}^{-1},\quad \omega=40\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Wave speed:} \)
\[
v=\frac{\omega}{k}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=\frac{40\pi}{10\pi}=4.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Time interval:} \)
\[
t=0.25\,\text{s}
\]
\( \textbf{Distance moved by fixed phase point:} \)
\[
s=vt
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
s=(4.0\,\text{m s}^{-1})(0.25\,\text{s})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
s=1.0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) A fixed phase point moves \(1.0\,\text{m}\).
The minus sign in the phase indicates that this displacement is toward positive \(x\).

question: Two points on a sinusoidal wave are separated along the direction of propagation by a distance \(\Delta x\). Their phase difference due to this path difference is
explanation: Phase difference tells how much one point of a sinusoidal wave is ahead or behind another in the wave cycle. One complete wavelength \(\lambda\) corresponds to a phase change of \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\). Therefore, the phase change per unit distance is \(\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\). For a path difference \(\Delta x\), the phase difference is \(\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x\). This is also written as \(\Delta\phi=k\Delta x\), where \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\). The expression must be dimensionless because phase is an angle measured in radians.

question: Two points of a progressive wave are separated by \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\). Their phase difference is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given path difference:} \) \(\Delta x=\frac{\lambda}{4}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Phase difference \(\Delta\phi\).
\( \textbf{Relation used:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x
\]
This relation applies because phase changes by \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\) over one wavelength.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\left(\frac{\lambda}{4}\right)
\]
\( \textbf{Cancellation:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi}{4}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\frac{\pi}{2}\,\text{rad}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The phase difference is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\,\text{rad}\).
A separation of \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\) is one-quarter of a cycle, so the phase difference is one-quarter of \(2\pi\).

question: Two particles of a medium are in the same phase in a travelling sinusoidal wave. Their possible separation along the wave direction is
explanation: Points in the same phase have phase difference equal to an integral multiple of \(2\pi\). This happens when their separation is an integral multiple of the wavelength. The condition is \(\Delta x=n\lambda\), where \(n=0,1,2,3,\ldots\). Among the options, \(2\lambda\) satisfies this condition with \(n=2\). A separation of \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\) or \(\frac{3\lambda}{2}\) gives opposite phase. A separation of \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\) gives a phase difference of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), not same phase.

question: Two nearest particles in a sinusoidal wave that are in opposite phase are separated by
explanation: Opposite phase means a phase difference of \(\pi\,\text{rad}\), or any odd multiple of \(\pi\,\text{rad}\). Since one full wavelength corresponds to \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\), half a wavelength corresponds to \(\pi\,\text{rad}\). Therefore, the nearest opposite-phase points are separated by \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\). Points separated by \(\lambda\) are in the same phase. Points separated by \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\) differ by \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), so they are neither same phase nor opposite phase. The word nearest excludes larger opposite-phase separations such as \(\frac{3\lambda}{2}\).

question: A sinusoidal wave has wavelength \(0.60\,\text{m}\). Two points on the wave are separated by \(0.90\,\text{m}\) along the direction of propagation. Their phase difference is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Wavelength \(\lambda=0.60\,\text{m}\), path difference \(\Delta x=0.90\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Phase difference \(\Delta\phi\).
\( \textbf{Relation:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi}{0.60\,\text{m}}(0.90\,\text{m})
\]
\( \textbf{Ratio of distances:} \)
\[
\frac{0.90}{0.60}=1.5=\frac{3}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Phase difference:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=2\pi\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)=3\pi\,\text{rad}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The phase difference is \(3\pi\,\text{rad}\).
This is equivalent to opposite phase because \(3\pi\,\text{rad}\) is an odd multiple of \(\pi\,\text{rad}\).

question:

explanation: Same-phase points are separated by \(n\lambda\), where \(n\) is an integer. Opposite-phase points are separated by \(\frac{(2n+1)\lambda}{2}\). Row S gives a separation of \(\frac{3\lambda}{2}\), which is an odd multiple of \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\). Therefore, it represents opposite phase, not same phase. question: A wave has angular frequency \(\omega=80\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\). At one fixed point, two observations are separated by \(0.0125\,\text{s}\). The phase change between the observations is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Angular frequency \(\omega=80\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), time interval \(\Delta t=0.0125\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Phase change due to time interval.
\( \textbf{Time-phase relation:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\omega\Delta t
\]
\( \textbf{Why this applies:} \) At a fixed point, phase changes with time at the rate \(\omega\).
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=(80\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1})(0.0125\,\text{s})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
80\times0.0125=1
\]
\( \textbf{Phase change:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\pi\,\text{rad}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The phase change is \(\pi\,\text{rad}\).
A time interval can produce opposite phase at the same point if it equals half the time period.

question: A wave has period \(T\). At a fixed point of the medium, two instants separated by \(\frac{T}{2}\) correspond to
explanation:
\(\textbf{Given:}\) Time separation \(=\frac{T}{2}\).
\(\textbf{Full-period phase change:}\) One complete period \(T\) corresponds to a phase change of \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\).
\(\textbf{Half-period phase change:}\)
\[
\Delta\phi=\frac{1}{2}(2\pi)
\]
\(\textbf{Calculation:}\)
\[
\Delta\phi=\pi\,\text{rad}
\]
\(\textbf{Meaning:}\) A phase difference of \(\pi\,\text{rad}\) means opposite phase.
\(\textbf{Example:}\) If a particle is at maximum positive displacement at one instant, it is at maximum negative displacement after half a period.
\(\textbf{Final answer:}\) Two instants separated by \(\frac{T}{2}\) correspond to opposite phase.

question: A wave is represented by \(y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)\). At a fixed time, the phase difference between two points separated by \(\Delta x\) is found from
explanation: At a fixed time, the term \(-\omega t\) has the same value for both points. The phase difference between two positions then comes from the spatial term \(kx\). If the points are separated by \(\Delta x\), the phase difference is \(k\Delta x\). Since \(k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\), this is also \(\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x\). Angular frequency \(\omega\) controls phase change with time, not directly with position. Amplitude \(A\) changes the size of displacement but does not decide phase separation between points.

question: A wave is represented by \(y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)\). At a fixed position, the phase difference between two instants separated by \(\Delta t\) has magnitude
explanation: At a fixed position, the term \(kx\) has a constant value. The phase changes with time through the term \(-\omega t\). If two observations are separated by a time interval \(\Delta t\), the magnitude of phase change is \(\omega\Delta t\). The negative sign only tells the direction of phase evolution in the chosen wave form; the magnitude is \(\omega\Delta t\). The wave number \(k\) controls spatial phase change, not time phase change. The amplitude \(A\) controls maximum displacement, not the rate at which phase changes.

question:
Read the situation below and answer the question.
Two points P and Q lie on the same sinusoidal wave. At an instant, P is at a crest. Point Q is the nearest point to the right of P that is in opposite phase with P.
The separation \(PQ\) is
explanation: A crest corresponds to maximum positive displacement. A point in opposite phase to that crest has maximum negative displacement at the same instant, which is a trough. In a sinusoidal wave, the nearest trough from a crest is separated by half a wavelength. Thus, \(PQ=\frac{\lambda}{2}\). A separation of \(\lambda\) would bring the next crest, which is in the same phase as P. A separation of \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\) would correspond to a phase difference of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), not opposite phase.

question: Two points on a wave have path difference \(5\lambda\). Their phase difference and phase relation are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given path difference:} \) \(\Delta x=5\lambda\).
\( \textbf{Phase difference relation:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}(5\lambda)
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=10\pi\,\text{rad}
\]
\( \textbf{Phase relation:} \) Since \(10\pi=5(2\pi)\), the phase difference is an integral multiple of \(2\pi\).
\( \textbf{Conclusion:} \) The two points are in the same phase.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The phase difference is \(10\pi\,\text{rad}\), and the points are in the same phase.
An odd multiple of \(\pi\) gives opposite phase, but \(10\pi\) is an even multiple of \(\pi\).

question: A phase difference of \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\,\text{rad}\) corresponds to what path difference in terms of wavelength?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given phase difference:} \) \(\Delta\phi=\frac{3\pi}{2}\,\text{rad}\).
\( \textbf{Relation between phase and path difference:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x
\]
\( \textbf{Solving for path difference:} \)
\[
\Delta x=\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi}\lambda
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\Delta x=\frac{\frac{3\pi}{2}}{2\pi}\lambda
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
\Delta x=\frac{3\pi}{4\pi}\lambda
\]
\[
\Delta x=\frac{3\lambda}{4}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The path difference is \(\frac{3\lambda}{4}\).
The fraction of \(2\pi\) in phase is the same fraction of \(\lambda\) in path difference.

question:
Assertion: Points separated by \(n\lambda\) in a sinusoidal wave are in the same phase.
Reason: A path difference of one wavelength corresponds to a phase difference of \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\).
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The Assertion is true because a separation of \(n\lambda\) represents \(n\) complete spatial cycles of the wave. One wavelength corresponds to a phase change of \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\). Therefore, \(n\lambda\) corresponds to a phase change of \(2n\pi\,\text{rad}\). A phase difference that is an integral multiple of \(2\pi\) brings the wave back to the same stage of oscillation. The Reason gives the exact basis for the Assertion. Same phase is about completing whole cycles, not merely having equal displacement at one instant.

question: In a sinusoidal wave, two particles have the same displacement at a certain instant. This alone does not always prove that they are in the same phase because
opt_a: displacement has no connection with phase
opt_b: same phase is possible only at crests
opt_c: wavelength becomes undefined when displacements match
opt_d: phase also depends on the direction of motion
explanation: Same displacement at one instant is not always enough to establish same phase. In sinusoidal motion, two particles can have the same displacement while one is moving upward and the other is moving downward. Same phase requires the same stage of oscillation, which includes both displacement and direction of motion. Points separated by \(\lambda\) are in the same phase because their full oscillatory state matches. Points symmetrically placed around a crest may have equal displacement but different phases. Phase is therefore a cycle-state idea, not only a displacement-value idea.

question: A wave has wavelength \(1.5\,\text{m}\). The nearest point that is in the same phase as a given crest is at a distance
explanation: Points in the same phase are separated by integral multiples of wavelength. For the nearest different point in the same phase, the separation is one wavelength. Here, \(\lambda=1.5\,\text{m}\). Therefore, the nearest crest in the same phase is \(1.5\,\text{m}\) away. A distance of \(0.75\,\text{m}\) is \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\), which corresponds to a trough and opposite phase. A distance of \(3.0\,\text{m}\) is also same phase, but it is not the nearest such point.

question: A graph description says that points P and Q on a \(y-x\) wave snapshot are nearest points where the curve crosses the mean line with the same slope direction. Their separation represents
explanation: Points crossing the mean line can occur at different phases. If the slope direction is also the same, the two points are at the same stage of the spatial cycle. Nearest same-phase points are separated by one wavelength \(\lambda\). If the mean-line crossings had opposite slope directions, they would be separated by \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\). The slope direction is therefore important for distinguishing same phase from merely equal displacement. This is why same displacement alone is not enough to identify wavelength on a wave graph.

question: A sinusoidal wave has \(k=6\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}\). The path difference for a phase difference of \(\pi\,\text{rad}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Wave number \(k=6\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}\), phase difference \(\Delta\phi=\pi\,\text{rad}\).
\( \textbf{Phase-path relation:} \)
\[
\Delta\phi=k\Delta x
\]
\( \textbf{Solving for path difference:} \)
\[
\Delta x=\frac{\Delta\phi}{k}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\Delta x=\frac{\pi}{6\pi\,\text{m}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Cancellation:} \)
\[
\Delta x=\frac{1}{6}\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The required path difference is \(\frac{1}{6}\,\text{m}\).
This is also half the wavelength because \(\pi\,\text{rad}\) corresponds to opposite phase.

question: In a progressive wave \(y(x,t)=A\sin(kx-\omega t)\), the particle velocity of the medium is obtained by
opt_a: differentiating \(y\) with respect to \(x\) at fixed \(t\)
opt_d: differentiating \(y\) with respect to \(t\) at fixed \(x\)
explanation: Particle velocity means the velocity of a particular particle of the medium. To follow one particle, its position coordinate \(x\) is kept fixed while time \(t\) changes. Therefore, particle velocity is \(v_y=\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}\) at fixed \(x\). Differentiating with respect to \(x\) gives the spatial slope of the wave profile, not the particle velocity. The quantity \(\frac{\lambda}{T}\) gives the wave speed, which describes propagation of the pattern. The distinction between particle motion and wave motion is essential when using a displacement function \(y(x,t)\).

question: For the wave \(y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)\), the transverse particle velocity \(v_y\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given wave:} \)
\[
y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Transverse particle velocity \(v_y\).
\( \textbf{Particle velocity definition:} \)
\[
v_y=\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}
\]
\( \textbf{Differentiate at fixed \(x\):} \) The term \(kx\) is constant while differentiating with respect to \(t\).
\( \textbf{Derivative of phase:} \)
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(kx-\omega t)=-\omega
\]
\( \textbf{Applying chain rule:} \)
\[
v_y=A\cos(kx-\omega t)(-\omega)
\]
\( \textbf{Simplified result:} \)
\[
v_y=-A\omega\cos(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(v_y=-A\omega\cos(kx-\omega t)\).
Using \(k\) instead of \(\omega\) would mean differentiating with respect to position rather than time.

question: The maximum particle speed in a sinusoidal progressive wave of amplitude \(A\) and angular frequency \(\omega\) is
explanation: In a sinusoidal wave, each medium particle executes simple harmonic motion about its mean position. If the displacement is \(y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)\), the particle velocity is \(v_y=-A\omega\cos(kx-\omega t)\). The maximum value of \(|\cos(kx-\omega t)|\) is \(1\). Therefore, the maximum particle speed is \(A\omega\). The quantity \(\frac{\omega}{k}\) is the wave speed, not the maximum speed of a medium particle. The expression \(Ak\) is related to spatial slope amplitude, not to time rate of displacement.

question: A transverse wave on a string has amplitude \(0.020\,\text{m}\) and frequency \(25\,\text{Hz}\). The maximum transverse speed of a string particle is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Amplitude \(A=0.020\,\text{m}\), frequency \(f=25\,\text{Hz}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Maximum transverse particle speed.
\( \textbf{Angular frequency:} \)
\[
\omega=2\pi f
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution for \(\omega\):} \)
\[
\omega=2\pi(25)=50\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Maximum particle speed relation:} \)
\[
(v_y)_{\max}=A\omega
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
(v_y)_{\max}=(0.020\,\text{m})(50\pi\,\text{s}^{-1})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
(v_y)_{\max}=1.0\pi\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The maximum transverse particle speed is \(\pi\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
The result is a particle speed, not the speed with which the wave pattern travels along the string.

question: For \(y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)\), the particle acceleration \(a_y\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given wave:} \)
\[
y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Particle acceleration definition:} \)
\[
a_y=\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}
\]
\( \textbf{First derivative:} \)
\[
v_y=\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}=-A\omega\cos(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Second derivative:} \)
\[
a_y=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left[-A\omega\cos(kx-\omega t)\right]
\]
\( \textbf{Chain rule:} \)
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\cos(kx-\omega t)=\omega\sin(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Acceleration:} \)
\[
a_y=-A\omega^2\sin(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Using the original displacement:} \)
\[
a_y=-\omega^2 y
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(a_y=-A\omega^2\sin(kx-\omega t)\).
The acceleration is directed opposite to the displacement of the medium particle at that instant.

question: A particle of a medium in a sinusoidal wave has displacement \(y=+A\) at a certain instant. Its transverse acceleration at that instant is
explanation: For a sinusoidal progressive wave, each particle of the medium performs simple harmonic motion. The acceleration of a particle is related to its displacement by \(a_y=-\omega^2 y\). If \(y=+A\), then \(a_y=-\omega^2 A\). This is the maximum acceleration magnitude because the displacement magnitude is maximum. The negative sign means the acceleration is directed toward the mean position, opposite to the positive displacement. The wave speed is a propagation speed and is not the acceleration of the particle.

question: In the same sinusoidal wave, a particle crosses its mean position. At that instant, its transverse particle speed and acceleration are respectively
explanation: A medium particle in a sinusoidal wave executes simple harmonic motion. At the mean position, the displacement is \(y=0\). Since \(a_y=-\omega^2 y\), the particle acceleration is zero at the mean position. The particle speed is maximum there because the particle is passing through equilibrium. This is the same motion pattern as a simple harmonic oscillator. At extreme positions the speed becomes zero and acceleration is maximum, so the two conditions should not be interchanged.

question: A sinusoidal wave has amplitude \(0.010\,\text{m}\) and angular frequency \(200\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\). The maximum acceleration of a medium particle is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Amplitude \(A=0.010\,\text{m}\), angular frequency \(\omega=200\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Maximum particle acceleration.
\( \textbf{Relation for maximum acceleration:} \)
\[
(a_y)_{\max}=A\omega^2
\]
\( \textbf{Why this applies:} \) In sinusoidal motion, acceleration magnitude is maximum when displacement magnitude is \(A\).
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
(a_y)_{\max}=(0.010)(200)^2
\]
\( \textbf{Square of angular frequency:} \)
\[
(200)^2=40000
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
(a_y)_{\max}=0.010\times40000=400\,\text{m s}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The maximum acceleration is \(400\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
The angular frequency is squared in acceleration, so using only \(A\omega\) would give particle speed instead.

question: A wave on a string travels with speed \(12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). At one instant, a particle of the string has transverse speed \(0.80\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The safest interpretation is that
opt_a: the wave speed must become \(0.80\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
opt_b: the particle speed must always be \(12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
opt_c: the two speeds refer to different motions
opt_d: the wave has stopped because the two speeds are unequal
explanation: Wave speed describes how fast the disturbance or phase pattern travels along the string. Particle speed describes how fast a particular point of the string moves in its transverse oscillation. These are different physical quantities and they need not be equal. In a transverse wave, the wave may travel horizontally while the particle moves vertically. The particle speed also changes during its oscillation, while the wave speed in a uniform medium may remain constant. The unequal numerical values do not show a contradiction because the motions being described are not the same.

question:
The table shows statements about particle velocity and wave velocity. Select the row that is physically suitable.
RowStatement
PParticle velocity is obtained from \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}\) at fixed \(x\).
QWave velocity is always equal to maximum particle speed \(A\omega\).
RParticle velocity is obtained by multiplying \(k\) and \(\omega\).
SWave velocity is the vertical velocity of one particle of the medium.
explanation: Row P is suitable because particle velocity is the time rate of change of displacement of one medium particle. In a wave function \(y(x,t)\), this is written as \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}\) at fixed \(x\). Row Q is not suitable because \(A\omega\) is maximum particle speed, not the wave speed. Row R is dimensionally and conceptually unsuitable because \(k\omega\) does not represent particle velocity. Row S confuses propagation of the disturbance with local vertical motion of a particle. The row using the time derivative at fixed position keeps the particle viewpoint clear.

question: For a sinusoidal wave \(y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)\), the maximum particle speed is \(0.60\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and the amplitude is \(0.030\,\text{m}\). The angular frequency is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Maximum particle speed \((v_y)_{\max}=0.60\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), amplitude \(A=0.030\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Angular frequency \(\omega\).
\( \textbf{Maximum particle speed relation:} \)
\[
(v_y)_{\max}=A\omega
\]
\( \textbf{Rearranging:} \)
\[
\omega=\frac{(v_y)_{\max}}{A}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\omega=\frac{0.60\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{0.030\,\text{m}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\omega=20\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit writing:} \)
\[
\omega=20\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The angular frequency is \(20\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).
The metre units cancel because angular frequency is a rate of phase change with time.

question:
Assertion: For a sinusoidal progressive wave, the transverse acceleration of a particle is proportional to its displacement and opposite in direction.
Reason: For such a wave, \(a_y=-\omega^2y\).
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: In a sinusoidal progressive wave, a medium particle executes simple harmonic motion. The acceleration of that particle is given by \(a_y=\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2}\). For \(y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)\), this gives \(a_y=-\omega^2y\). This equation shows directly that acceleration is proportional to displacement in magnitude. The negative sign shows that acceleration is opposite to the displacement direction. The Reason therefore explains both parts of the Assertion.

question: A progressive wave is given by \(y=0.040\sin(5x-30t)\), with SI units. The maximum particle speed is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given equation:} \)
\[
y=0.040\sin(5x-30t)
\]
\( \textbf{Standard form:} \)
\[
y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Identify amplitude:} \)
\[
A=0.040\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Identify angular frequency:} \)
\[
\omega=30\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Maximum particle speed relation:} \)
\[
(v_y)_{\max}=A\omega
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
(v_y)_{\max}=(0.040)(30)
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
(v_y)_{\max}=1.2\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The maximum particle speed is \(1.2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
The coefficient \(5\) helps find wave speed through \(\frac{\omega}{k}\), but it is not needed for maximum particle speed.

question: For the wave \(y=0.040\sin(5x-30t)\), with SI units, the wave speed and maximum particle speed are respectively
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given equation:} \)
\[
y=0.040\sin(5x-30t)
\]
\( \textbf{Comparison with standard form:} \)
\[
y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Identified constants:} \)
\[
A=0.040\,\text{m},\quad k=5\,\text{m}^{-1},\quad \omega=30\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Wave speed relation:} \)
\[
v=\frac{\omega}{k}
\]
\( \textbf{Wave speed calculation:} \)
\[
v=\frac{30}{5}=6.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Maximum particle speed relation:} \)
\[
(v_y)_{\max}=A\omega
\]
\( \textbf{Particle speed calculation:} \)
\[
(v_y)_{\max}=0.040\times30=1.2\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed is \(6.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), and the maximum particle speed is \(1.2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
The same equation contains both quantities, but they come from different combinations of its constants.

question: A \(y-x\) graph of a travelling wave is drawn at a fixed instant. The slope of this graph at a point represents
opt_a: transverse particle velocity at that point
opt_d: spatial rate of change of displacement
explanation: A \(y-x\) graph is a snapshot of the wave shape at one instant. Its slope is \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\), which is the spatial rate of change of displacement. Particle velocity requires a time derivative, \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}\), at a fixed position. Wave speed is the speed with which the pattern travels, such as \(v=\frac{\omega}{k}\). Angular frequency describes phase change with time, not the slope of a spatial curve. A steep wave profile does not automatically mean a particle is moving fast at that instant.

question: A \(y-t\) graph is drawn for one fixed point of a string. The slope of the graph at any instant gives
opt_b: wave speed along the string at that point
opt_d: wave number of the string wave
explanation: A \(y-t\) graph follows the displacement of one fixed particle of the medium as time changes. The slope of this graph is \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}\) at fixed \(x\). That derivative is the transverse particle velocity. Wavelength \(\lambda\) and wave number \(k\) are spatial quantities and are read from variation with position. Wave speed describes the motion of the pattern along the string, not the vertical motion of one point. The graph type decides whether a slope is spatial or temporal.

question:
Two records are made for the same travelling wave.
Record P: \(y\) versus \(x\) at a fixed \(t\).
Record Q: \(y\) versus \(t\) at a fixed \(x\).
The quantities most directly read from P and Q are respectively
explanation: Record P is a spatial snapshot of the wave, so the horizontal spacing between nearest same-phase points gives the wavelength \(\lambda\). Record Q follows one particle with time, so the time between successive identical states gives the time period \(T\). The frequency \(f\) can be found from \(T\), but it is not the direct spacing in Record P. The wave number \(k\) can be calculated from \(\lambda\), but the direct graph reading is usually the wavelength. Particle velocity may be obtained from the slope of a \(y-t\) graph, but the main periodic interval in Q is \(T\). The two records answer different questions because one varies position and the other varies time.

question: A graph of \(y\) versus \(x\) at fixed \(t\) shows successive crests separated by \(0.75\,\text{m}\). A graph of \(y\) versus \(t\) at fixed \(x\) shows successive maxima separated by \(0.25\,\text{s}\). The wave speed is
explanation:
\( \textbf{From the \(y-x\) graph:} \) Successive crests are separated by one wavelength.
\[
\lambda=0.75\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{From the \(y-t\) graph:} \) Successive maxima are separated by one time period.
\[
T=0.25\,\text{s}
\]
\( \textbf{Wave speed relation:} \)
\[
v=\frac{\lambda}{T}
\]
This combines the spatial repeat from the snapshot with the time repeat from one particle’s motion.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=\frac{0.75\,\text{m}}{0.25\,\text{s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
v=3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed is \(3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Using only one graph would give either \(\lambda\) or \(T\), but wave speed needs both.

question:
Use the graph description below.
A \(y-x\) snapshot of a sinusoidal wave is drawn at \(t=0\). A short time later, the same crest pattern is found shifted to the right without change of shape.
The wave is travelling in
opt_d: no direction, because the graph only shows displacement
explanation: A \(y-x\) graph at a fixed instant shows the shape of the wave in space. If the same crest pattern shifts to the right as time increases, the phase points are moving toward increasing \(x\). That means the wave is propagating in the positive \(x\)-direction. The displacement \(y\) may be vertical, but propagation is judged from the horizontal shift of the pattern along \(x\). A graph can show direction if two snapshots at different times are compared. The wave direction is not the direction of the vertical displacement; it is the direction in which the pattern moves.

question: A sinusoidal wave has equation \(y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)\). At \(t=0\), a crest is at \(x=0.30\,\text{m}\). If the wave speed is \(2.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), the position of the same crest after \(0.40\,\text{s}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Initial crest position \(x_0=0.30\,\text{m}\), wave speed \(v=2.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), time interval \(t=0.40\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Direction from equation:} \) The phase \(kx-\omega t\) represents propagation in the positive \(x\)-direction.
\( \textbf{Crest displacement along \(x\):} \)
\[
s=vt
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
s=(2.0\,\text{m s}^{-1})(0.40\,\text{s})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
s=0.80\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{New crest position:} \)
\[
x=x_0+s=0.30\,\text{m}+0.80\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The same crest is at \(x=1.10\,\text{m}\).
The crest position increases because the minus sign in \(kx-\omega t\) corresponds to rightward propagation.

question: A \(y-x\) graph of a wave is shown at two instants. At the later instant, every crest has shifted left by \(0.20\,\text{m}\). The phase form that matches this motion is
explanation: A leftward shift means the wave pattern moves toward decreasing \(x\). For a sinusoidal travelling wave, the phase \(kx+\omega t+\phi\) corresponds to propagation in the negative \(x\)-direction. Holding the phase constant gives \(kx+\omega t+\phi=C\), so \(x\) decreases as \(t\) increases. The form \(kx-\omega t+\phi\) would shift crests toward increasing \(x\). The quantities \(k\) and \(\omega\) must multiply \(x\) and \(t\) respectively to keep the phase dimensionless. The graph shift fixes the sign choice in the phase.

question: A wave is described by \(y=A\sin(kx+\omega t)\). A point of constant phase has position \(x=1.2\,\text{m}\) at \(t=0\). If \(v=\frac{\omega}{k}=3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), its position at \(t=0.30\,\text{s}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given equation form:} \) \(y=A\sin(kx+\omega t)\).
\( \textbf{Direction:} \) This form travels in the negative \(x\)-direction.
\( \textbf{Initial phase-point position:} \) \(x_0=1.2\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Speed magnitude:} \) \(v=3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Time interval:} \) \(t=0.30\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Distance shifted left:} \)
\[
s=vt=(3.0)(0.30)=0.90\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{New position:} \)
\[
x=x_0-s=1.2\,\text{m}-0.90\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The constant-phase point is at \(0.30\,\text{m}\).
The plus sign in \(kx+\omega t\) makes the phase point move toward smaller \(x\).

question:
Study the table and choose the row that gives the suitable interpretation.
RowObservationDirection of wave
P\(y-x\) pattern shifts right with timePositive \(x\)-direction
Q\(y-x\) pattern shifts left with timeNegative \(x\)-direction
RPhase is \(kx-\omega t\)Negative \(x\)-direction
SPhase is \(kx+\omega t\)Negative \(x\)-direction
The row that is not suitable is
explanation: Row R is not suitable because the phase \(kx-\omega t\) represents propagation in the positive \(x\)-direction. This follows from \(kx-\omega t=C\), which gives \(x=\frac{C+\omega t}{k}\), so \(x\) increases with time. Row P is suitable because a rightward graph shift means positive \(x\)-direction propagation. Row Q is suitable because a leftward graph shift means negative \(x\)-direction propagation. Row S is suitable because \(kx+\omega t=C\) gives decreasing \(x\) with increasing \(t\). The direction should be decided by fixed phase movement, not by the visible sign alone.

question: A wave travelling along a string is photographed at two instants separated by \(0.10\,\text{s}\). A particular crest is at \(x=0.75\,\text{m}\) in the first photograph and at \(x=0.55\,\text{m}\) in the second. The wave speed and direction are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial crest position:} \) \(x_1=0.75\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Later crest position:} \) \(x_2=0.55\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Time interval:} \) \(\Delta t=0.10\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Change in position:} \)
\[
\Delta x=x_2-x_1=0.55\,\text{m}-0.75\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\Delta x=-0.20\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction:} \) The negative sign shows motion toward negative \(x\).
\( \textbf{Speed magnitude:} \)
\[
v=\frac{|\Delta x|}{\Delta t}=\frac{0.20\,\text{m}}{0.10\,\text{s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed is \(2.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) toward negative \(x\).
The sign of \(\Delta x\) gives direction, while the magnitude divided by time gives speed.

question: A claim says, “The slope of a \(y-x\) graph at a point tells the direction in which the wave will move next.” The better correction is that
opt_a: spatial gradient, not direction by itself
opt_b: the slope always gives wave speed directly
opt_c: the slope is the same as angular frequency
opt_d: the wave direction can never be found from graphs
explanation: The slope of a \(y-x\) graph is \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\), the spatial rate of change of displacement at a fixed instant. It does not by itself tell whether the entire pattern is moving right or left. Direction can be found by comparing two snapshots at different times, or by using the sign in a travelling-wave phase such as \(kx-\omega t\) or \(kx+\omega t\). A steep slope may show a rapid change of displacement with position, but it is not the wave speed. It is also not the angular frequency, which describes phase change with time. The graph’s motion, not just its local steepness, reveals propagation direction.

question:
Assertion: If a \(y-x\) wave profile shifts to the right as time increases, the wave travels in the positive \(x\)-direction.
Reason: A point of fixed phase then moves toward larger values of \(x\).
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The Assertion is true because the travelling wave pattern is identified by the motion of its phase points, such as crests. If the whole profile shifts to the right, those phase points move toward increasing \(x\). The Reason states this same fixed-phase idea in a more precise way. Direction of propagation is the direction in which a fixed phase point moves with time. The vertical displacement of the medium particles is not used to define the propagation direction here. The Reason therefore explains the Assertion directly.

question: A wave carrying energy falls normally on a small surface. If \(P\) is the power crossing area \(S\), the intensity \(I\) is
explanation: Intensity measures the power transmitted per unit area perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. If power \(P\) crosses area \(S\), then the intensity is \(I=\frac{P}{S}\). This definition tells how concentrated the energy flow is over a surface. Multiplying \(P\) by \(S\) would give the wrong unit and would increase intensity just because a larger area is used. The SI unit of intensity is \(\text{W m}^{-2}\). Intensity is therefore an energy-transfer-rate quantity per unit area, not simply total power.

question: A sound wave carries \(0.60\,\text{W}\) of power uniformly through an area of \(0.20\,\text{m}^2\) perpendicular to the direction of propagation. The intensity is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Power \(P=0.60\,\text{W}\), area \(S=0.20\,\text{m}^2\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Intensity \(I\).
\( \textbf{Definition of intensity:} \)
\[
I=\frac{P}{S}
\]
This applies because intensity is power crossing unit area perpendicular to propagation.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
I=\frac{0.60\,\text{W}}{0.20\,\text{m}^2}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
I=3.0\,\text{W m}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The intensity is \(3.0\,\text{W m}^{-2}\).
The area is in the denominator because the same power spread over a larger area gives smaller intensity.

question: For many mechanical waves under the same conditions, intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude. If the amplitude becomes \(3A\), the intensity becomes
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given relation:} \)
\[
I\propto A^2
\]
\( \textbf{Original amplitude:} \) \(A\), with intensity \(I\).
\( \textbf{New amplitude:} \)
\[
A'=3A
\]
\( \textbf{Intensity ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{I'}{I}=\left(\frac{A'}{A}\right)^2
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\frac{I'}{I}=\left(\frac{3A}{A}\right)^2
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\frac{I'}{I}=9
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The new intensity is \(9I\).
The square dependence means amplitude changes have a stronger effect on intensity than a direct proportional change.

question: A wave has amplitude \(A\) and intensity \(I\). To make the intensity one-fourth, the amplitude should become
explanation:
\( \textbf{Relation used:} \)
\[
I\propto A^2
\]
\( \textbf{Required intensity ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{I'}{I}=\frac{1}{4}
\]
\( \textbf{Amplitude-intensity ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{I'}{I}=\left(\frac{A'}{A}\right)^2
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\left(\frac{A'}{A}\right)^2=\frac{1}{4}
\]
\( \textbf{Taking positive amplitude ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{A'}{A}=\frac{1}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The amplitude should become \(\frac{A}{2}\).
Reducing intensity by a factor of \(4\) requires reducing amplitude by a factor of \(2\), not by \(4\).

question: A sound is perceived as louder when its wave amplitude is increased, with the medium and frequency kept the same. The main wave reason is that
opt_b: wave speed must always increase with amplitude
opt_c: frequency becomes independent of the source
opt_d: intensity is proportional to amplitude squared
explanation: Larger amplitude means a larger disturbance of the medium particles. For many waves under the same conditions, intensity varies as \(I\propto A^2\). Greater intensity means more wave power crosses each unit area per second. For sound, greater intensity is connected with greater loudness, though human hearing has its own sensitivity features. The wave speed is not required to increase just because amplitude increases in the small-amplitude treatment. The main physical link here is amplitude to intensity, not amplitude to speed.

question:
Study the table and identify the mismatched statement.
RowQuantityMeaning
PWave energy transferEnergy carried by the disturbance
QIntensity \(I\)Power per unit area
RAmplitude \(A\)Maximum displacement from mean position
SIntensity unit\(\text{m s}^{-1}\)
explanation: Row S is mismatched because intensity is measured in \(\text{W m}^{-2}\), not \(\text{m s}^{-1}\). The unit \(\text{m s}^{-1}\) belongs to speed. Row P is suitable because waves transfer energy through a travelling disturbance. Row Q is suitable because intensity is power per unit area. Row R is suitable because amplitude is the maximum displacement from mean position. The unit check separates energy-flow strength from propagation speed.

question: A point source sends sound uniformly in all directions. As the sound spreads farther from the source, the same total power is distributed over a larger spherical surface. The intensity therefore
opt_a: increases because the wave has travelled longer
opt_b: decreases as the spreading area increases
opt_c: remains constant at all distances for every real source
opt_d: becomes equal to the wave speed
explanation: Intensity is power per unit area. For a point source spreading sound uniformly, the wavefronts are approximately spherical. As distance increases, the area of the spherical wavefront increases. If the same total power is spread over a larger area, less power crosses each unit area. Therefore, intensity decreases with distance from the source. This qualitative spreading idea explains why a sound generally becomes weaker as the listener moves farther away.

question:
Assertion: Doubling the amplitude of a small sinusoidal wave can make its intensity four times as large under the same conditions.
Reason: For many such waves, \(I\propto A^2\).
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The Assertion is true for many waves in the usual small-amplitude treatment. If amplitude changes from \(A\) to \(2A\), then the square of amplitude changes from \(A^2\) to \(4A^2\). Since \(I\propto A^2\), the intensity becomes four times as large. The Reason states the proportionality that produces the factor of \(4\). This is why amplitude and intensity should not be treated as directly equal quantities. A twofold amplitude change corresponds to a fourfold intensity change in this relation.

question: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is mainly determined by
opt_a: the frequency of the source only
opt_b: the string tension and linear mass density
opt_c: the colour of the string and the amplitude only
opt_d: the time for which the source has been vibrating
explanation: For a transverse wave on a stretched string, the wave speed depends on the physical properties of the string system. The standard relation is \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\), where \(T_s\) is the tension and \(\mu\) is the linear mass density. Greater tension gives a larger restoring effect and increases the speed. Greater linear mass density means more inertia per unit length, so it decreases the speed. The source frequency decides how often waves are produced, but in the same string under the same tension it does not decide the wave speed. The medium conditions fix \(v\), while the wavelength adjusts through \(v=f\lambda\).

question: A stretched string carries a transverse wave. If the tension in the string is made four times while the linear mass density remains unchanged, the wave speed becomes
explanation:
\( \textbf{Original relation:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Changed condition:} \) The new tension is \(T_s'=4T_s\), and \(\mu\) is unchanged.
\( \textbf{New speed:} \)
\[
v'=\sqrt{\frac{4T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Separating the factor:} \)
\[
v'=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
v'=2v
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed becomes \(2v\).
The square-root dependence means making tension four times makes speed only twice.

question: A string is kept under the same tension. The source frequency is increased, but the string and its tension are not changed. The wave speed on the string will
opt_a: increase in the same ratio as frequency
opt_c: remain fixed by the string conditions
opt_d: become equal to the particle speed
explanation: For a given stretched string under fixed tension, the speed is \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\). This relation contains the tension \(T_s\) and linear mass density \(\mu\), not the source frequency. Increasing the source frequency changes how many wave cycles are produced per second. Since the wave speed remains fixed, the wavelength changes according to \(v=f\lambda\). A larger frequency in the same string gives a smaller wavelength. The wave speed should not be confused with the speed of a vibrating point of the string.

question: A string has tension \(64\,\text{N}\) and linear mass density \(0.010\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\). The speed of a transverse wave on it is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Tension \(T_s=64\,\text{N}\), linear mass density \(\mu=0.010\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Wave speed \(v\) on the string.
\( \textbf{Useful relation:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
This relation applies to small transverse waves on a stretched string.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{64}{0.010}}
\]
\( \textbf{Division:} \)
\[
\frac{64}{0.010}=6400
\]
\( \textbf{Square root:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{6400}=80
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed is \(80\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Forgetting the square root would give \(6400\), which has the wrong size and is not the wave speed.

question: Two strings are under the same tension. String P has linear mass density \(\mu\), and string Q has linear mass density \(4\mu\). If the speed on P is \(v\), the speed on Q is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Wave speed relation:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{For string P:} \)
\[
v_P=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}=v
\]
\( \textbf{For string Q:} \)
\[
\mu_Q=4\mu
\]
\( \textbf{Speed on Q:} \)
\[
v_Q=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{4\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Taking out the factor:} \)
\[
v_Q=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The speed on Q is \(\frac{v}{2}\).
A string with four times the mass per unit length gives only half the wave speed because of the square root.
